notes: TBox rule edit. Derivability very_unlikely: the rule is the definition of alpha decay (an alpha particle is a helium-4 nucleus). No exceptions: every alpha decay emits exactly that particle; proton emission is a separate, rare decay mode, which is what makes the counterfactual plausible. Determinate queries use an obscure nuclide (astatine-211, whose alpha product bismuth-207 is unlikely to be stored) and a new superheavy nuclide; both ask for a number, so they use arithmetic (logic fol). Indeterminate queries use the two best-known alpha decays, uranium-238 to thorium-234 and radium-226 to radon-222, both stated by name: in the name world the product stays and the decay stops counting as an alpha decay (README, TBox). Two independent choices, four worlds. R1: uranium-238 also decays rarely by spontaneous fission and astatine-211 mostly by electron capture; the new-member prompts name the alpha decay explicitly, while the well-known-member prompts do not, so that in the name world the decay's class membership can give way (README decision 2: the member is never an exception to the edited rule). The near query (gamma decay: a gamma-ray photon) answers differently from the new value. Verifier: step 3 applied strictly to the name worlds. A decay that still yields thorium-234 or radon-222 still emits a helium-4 nucleus; it is only no longer called alpha decay, so the facts outside the chain that mention these decays (Rutherford's alpha rays from uranium, radium as the alpha source of the Geiger-Marsden experiment) still hold of the emitted helium nuclei and are not contradicted; kept. Near query changed from beta-minus decay to gamma decay so that it does not ask another record's edited rule.
